Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

Screw Threads

Choose a thread form for the load, read an inch or metric callout, and identify which way a screw advances.

A fastener holds parts together; a power screw moves a load

A fastener holds parts together; a power screw moves a load

A thread is a ridge wrapped around a cylinder. A matching internal thread in a nut follows that ridge. Relative rotation can produce straight-line travel along the screw's axis.

A machine screw usually holds parts together. A lead screw uses the thread to position or drive a load: a slide, a vise jaw, or a linear actuator. Belts, chains and gears commonly transfer rotation between shafts; a lead screw converts rotation into linear motion. See Lead Screws for the calculations.

Keep four descriptions separate: form is the thread's cross-sectional shape; series selects diameter and pitch combinations; hand determines direction; starts count the separate helices. A helix is the spiral path around the cylinder.

Match the thread form to fastening, repeated travel, or one-way thrust

Match the thread form to fastening, repeated travel, or one-way thrust

Thread-form trade-offs for sliding screw-and-nut contact.
Form and useWhat it offersWhat it costs
Square: power screws and jacksHigh efficiency relative to angled flanks under otherwise comparable conditions.Difficult, expensive machining; wear adjustment is difficult.
V / machine-screw thread: bolts and fastening screwsWidely available fasteners; mass production by rolling makes standard parts economical.Flank wedging increases friction, so it is a poor choice for efficient repeated power transmission.
ACME / metric trapezoidal: vises, clamps and linear actuatorsEasier machining than square; a broader thread root provides a sturdier profile than a comparable square thread. Split-nut (an adjustable, divided nut) arrangements can take up clearance.Flank wedging increases friction relative to square. A precision drive screw can cost more than an ordinary stock fastener.
Buttress: heavy axial thrust (push along the screw) predominantly in one axial direction, such as a screw pressA nearly perpendicular working flank limits wedging in the intended load direction; the sloping back supports the thread.Its strength and efficiency advantages are directional. A special asymmetric profile and matching nut affect manufacturing and cost.

No thread form wins every comparison. Actual strength also depends on diameter, pitch, engaged length, material and the failure being checked. ACME is not automatically stronger than every V thread. Nor does its name guarantee a larger lead. ACME and metric trapezoidal are related forms, not interchangeable parts.

Supporting detail: Addendum 1 — Why the efficiency and strength comparisons need conditions.

No radial wedging (outward force on the nut) does not mean no wear

No radial wedging (outward force on the nut) does not mean no wear

In the ideal square-thread geometry, axial load does not create the outward wedging associated with angled flanks. That reduces a source of radial loading on the nut. The loaded surfaces still slide against each other. Friction, lubrication, materials, load and speed still affect wear.

Wear can increase backlash: clearance that must be taken up after reversing direction before the load moves. An adjustable nut can reduce that clearance; adjustment does not restore lost material or guarantee longer life. Do not infer nut life from the thread profile alone.

Supporting detail: Addendum 2 — Where wear and operating limits enter the selection.

Inch callouts count threads; metric callouts state pitch; Practice

Inch callouts count threads; metric callouts state pitch

Pitch is the axial distance between adjacent thread crests. Inch fastener callouts commonly give threads per inch (TPI), so pitch = 1 / TPI in inches. Metric callouts give pitch directly in millimetres.

Selected callouts transcribed from checked public standard sources; pitches in the last column are calculated.
CalloutRead it asPitch
1/4-20 UNCNominal diameter 1/4 in; 20 threads per inch; Unified coarse series1/20 = 0.050 in
1/4-28 UNFNominal diameter 1/4 in; 28 threads per inch; Unified fine series1/28 ≈ 0.03571 in
M6 × 1.0Metric thread; nominal diameter 6 mm; pitch 1.0 mm1.0 mm

Fine means a smaller pitch at the same nominal diameter. It does not mean a better-quality thread. Metric threads also have coarse and fine pitch choices. The 6 in M6 is a diameter, not a pitch; the 20 in 1/4-20 is a count per inch, not a lead.

These are basic size-and-pitch callouts, not complete manufacturing specifications. Fit and tolerance information may follow them. A fastener-series label does not tell you the efficiency of a lead screw; for a multiple-start drive, obtain both pitch and starts, or the lead directly.

Supporting detail: Addendum 3 — The exact standard entries used here.

Practice reading an inch callout

Right-hand and left-hand threads advance in opposite directions

Right-hand and left-hand threads advance in opposite directions

Fix the nut and look along the screw from the end you turn. Clockwise turns a right-hand screw away from you into the nut. The same clockwise rotation moves a left-hand screw toward you. Reverse the rotation and the travel reverses.

If the screw is held against axial motion and the nut travels instead, the nut moves opposite to the screw travel just described. Handedness changes the direction, not the magnitude of travel per revolution.

Supporting detail: Addendum 4 — Direction reference.

Next, distinguish pitch from lead in Lead Screws.

Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

Lead Screws

Pitch times starts gives lead. Use lead to convert rpm into travel speed and torque into force, with efficiency applied only to the force conversion.

Pitch is thread spacing; lead is travel per revolution

Pitch is thread spacing; lead is travel per revolution

Lead = pitch × number of starts. This is the distinction to get right before calculating either speed or force.

A start is one continuous helical ridge. A single-start screw has one ridge, so its lead equals its pitch. A triple-start screw has three interleaved ridges: follow one ridge through a full turn and it advances three pitch distances.

At the same pitch, adding starts increases travel per turn. At the same torque it reduces theoretical force. The thread's cross-sectional form and its number of starts are separate choices; see Screw Threads.

Supporting detail: Addendum 5 — Check the definition, not just the label on a catalog.

Multiply rpm by lead to find linear speed

Multiply rpm by lead to find linear speed

For an engaged screw and nut, with the nut restrained from rotating, v = nL. Here n is screw speed in revolutions per minute and L is lead in distance per revolution. The result is distance per minute. Divide by 60 for distance per second.

A triple-start screw with 1.5 mm pitch has L = 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 mm/rev. At 480 rpm, v = 480 × 4.5 = 2,160 mm/min = 36 mm/s.

Do not multiply that speed by efficiency. The teaching rule is: “RPM → velocity is 100% efficient unless the screw is malfunctioning; all efficiency losses are found in the torque → force conversion.” This describes a positive-drive motion relationship, not 100% energy efficiency. It is the same tooth-count principle used in Gear Ratios.

Use the actual screw rpm. If the motor slows under load, the lower rpm gives a lower travel speed. Backlash at reversal and elastic deflection can affect positioning without being an efficiency factor on speed. These calculations describe steady engaged travel, after clearance is taken up. See Rotation and Linear Speed for the general rotation-to-travel connection.

Divide torque times 2π by lead, then apply efficiency

Divide torque times 2π by lead, then apply efficiency

For steady motion driving a resisting axial load, Ftheoretical = 2πT / L and Factual = η × Ftheoretical. Here T is input torque and η (eta) is efficiency written as a decimal: 40% is 0.40.

Make the length in torque match the length in lead.
TorqueLead for force calculationForce
N·mmetres per revolution (mm ÷ 1,000)N
lbf·in (often written lb-in)inches per revolutionlbf

To find the torque required for a target actual force, rearrange: T = FL / (2πη). For the same load and lead, lower efficiency requires more torque. Keep the efficiency boundary consistent: a whole screw assembly efficiency includes losses in the bearings or collar (a supporting thrust-contact surface) as well as the threads.

Supporting detail: Addendum 6 — Derive the 2π from equal power, or one revolution of work.

Experiment: more starts change speed and force in opposite ways; Interactive

Experiment: more starts change speed and force in opposite ways

Predict first: keep pitch, rpm, torque and efficiency fixed, then change from one start to three. Lead and speed triple; theoretical force falls to one third. The same force ratio holds when efficiency is held fixed.

Static comparison / print example: pitch 2 mm, 300 rpm, torque 1.2 N·m, given efficiency 40%.

Same pitch and input, different starts.

12 mm/rev10 mm/s3,770 N1,508 N

Changing efficiency to 20% halves each actual force; both speeds stay the same. Real efficiency can change with lead, lubrication and load. Here it is an independent input so the two effects can be studied separately.

Worked actuator: keep inch torque and inch lead together; Practice

Worked actuator: keep inch torque and inch lead together

A single-start ACME actuator has 0.20 in pitch, runs at 900 rpm and receives 12 lbf·in of torque. Its assembly efficiency is given as 60%. Find travel speed and useful axial force.

  1. L = 0.20 × 1 = 0.20 in/rev.
  2. v = 900 × 0.20 = 180 in/min = 3 in/s.
  3. Ftheoretical = 2π × 12 / 0.20 = 376.99 lbf.
  4. Factual = 376.99 × 0.60 ≈ 226 lbf.

The 60% belongs in step 4, not step 2. It is an example input, not an efficiency assigned to every ACME screw.

Practice actuator force

Worked vise: turn hand force into torque before finding clamp force; Practice

Worked vise: turn hand force into torque before finding clamp force

For an illustrative square-thread vise, a 120 N hand force acts perpendicular to the handle at a radius of 0.18 m from the screw axis. Pitch is 4 mm with one start. Assume a given overall tightening efficiency of 30%; this is not a measured or universal vise efficiency.

  1. Use torque = radius × perpendicular force: T = 0.18 × 120 = 21.6 N·m. Radius is the distance from the axis to the hand, not necessarily the full handle length.
  2. L = 4 mm/rev = 0.004 m/rev.
  3. Factual = 0.30 × 2π × 21.6 / 0.004 ≈ 10,179 N = 10.18 kN.

This is a tightening estimate using the supplied efficiency. It is not a vise rating or a prediction of residual force after the hand stops turning. A separate free-travel calculation at 24 rpm gives 24 × 4 / 60 = 1.6 mm/s; the jaws do not continue at that speed through a rigid clamped part.

Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

Backlash and Lost Motion

After a feed screw reverses, the handwheel turns through the thread clearance before the carriage moves. Predict that dead band from clearance and lead, and finish every approach in one direction.

The dial counts screw rotation; the indicator finds the carriage

The dial counts screw rotation; the indicator finds the carriage

A handwheel dial does not measure the carriage. It counts how far the screw has turned and multiplies by the lead. That is the carriage's travel only while the screw keeps pushing the nut in one direction.

A screw and its nut need some clearance between their thread flanks (a flank is the sloping side of a thread). After the screw changes direction, it must turn through that clearance before its other flank meets the nut and the carriage moves again. That clearance is backlash, the same idea defined for threads in Screw Threads and for gear teeth in Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry. The turn spent crossing it is lost motion: input that produces no output.

  • Dial reading: travel predicted from screw rotation, turns × lead. See Lead Screws.
  • Carriage position: where the carriage really is, as an indicator touching it would show.
  • The difference is zero after a forward approach (the direction the dial was zeroed in) and one full clearance after a reverse approach.

Supporting detail: Addendum 7 — Where the definition comes from.

Experiment: reverse the handwheel and watch the carriage wait; Interactive

Experiment: reverse the handwheel and watch the carriage wait

What the lab does: a handwheel turns an axially fixed lead screw. The dial reports travel calculated from screw rotation; an indicator on the carriage reports where the carriage really is. With a total axial clearance B between screw and nut flanks, the two agree only while the screw keeps pushing in the direction the dial was set in.

Dead band after a reversal = clearance ÷ lead, as a fraction of a turn:

angle = 360° × B ÷ L   dial divisions = B ÷ (L ÷ 100) on a dial with 100 divisions per turn.

Worked example: lead L = 5 mm/rev, so one division is 0.05 mm. Clearance B = 0.20 mm. Angle = 360° × 0.20 ÷ 5 = 14.4°; divisions = 0.20 ÷ 0.05 = 4. For four divisions after the reversal the dial changes and the carriage does not.

Landing on 25.00 mm after overshooting to 25.60 mm (lead 5 mm, clearance 0.20 mm). The dial was zeroed after a forward approach, so it equals the carriage position only for forward approaches:

Same dial number, two approaches.
MethodDial movesDialCarriageError
Reverse straight to the number25.60 → 25.00 mm25.00 mm25.20 mm+0.20 mm
Back past it, approach forward again25.60 → 24.50 → 25.00 mm25.00 mm25.00 mm0.00 mm

Reversing straight to the number stops the carriage one full clearance away from the dial reading, still on the overshoot side: the dial shows 25.00 mm while the carriage is at 25.20 mm. Backing past the target by more than the clearance and finishing in the original direction puts the screw back on the flank the dial was set against.

Model limits: rigid parts and a kinematic dead band only. Friction is assumed to hold the carriage still inside the clearance, and nothing else pushes it along the axis; there is no force, stiffness, preload or stick-slip model. Lead, clearance and the 3D dimensions are illustrative and exaggerated, not a standard thread or a measured machine.

Predict the dead band: clearance divided by lead, as a fraction of a turn

Predict the dead band: clearance divided by lead, as a fraction of a turn

Once the screw reverses, the carriage stays still until the screw's helix has moved one full clearance B. One turn moves the helix one lead L, so the dead band is B ÷ L of a turn.

dead-band angle = 360° × B ÷ L

dead-band divisions = B ÷ (value of one division); with 100 divisions per turn, one division is L ÷ 100.

Same clearance, two leads (illustrative values, 100-division dial).
Lead LOne divisionClearance BDead band
5 mm/rev0.05 mm0.20 mm4 divisions = 14.4°
2 mm/rev0.02 mm0.20 mm10 divisions = 36°

The carriage error after a reverse approach is the same 0.20 mm in both rows. A finer lead only spreads that same clearance over more of the handwheel turn.

Land on a dimension: finish every approach in the direction the dial was set

Land on a dimension: finish every approach in the direction the dial was set

If you overshoot a target, turning straight back to the number leaves the carriage one clearance away from it, because the screw is now pushing on the other flank. Instead:

  1. Back the handwheel past the target by more than the backlash.
  2. Turn in the original direction again and stop on the number.

The same reasoning applies when setting a dial. MIT's 2.670 milling notes say to “be certain that the backlash in the mechanism driving the table is taken up prior to setting the dial indicator”. A dial set with the clearance taken up in one direction reads true for approaches in that direction. For edge finding, Mill Indicators and Part Zero repeats the touch from the same direction for the same reason.

Supporting detail: Addendum 8 — A readout that measures the slide, and when the clearance still matters.

What the lab model includes and leaves out

What the lab model includes and leaves out

  • Included: a rigid screw that turns but never slides along its axis, a nut fixed to the carriage, and a total axial clearance B. The carriage position c stays within B/2 of the screw's helical phase s = −Lφ/360° (right-hand thread, φ the screw rotation); inside that band it does not move.
  • Assumed: friction holds the carriage still inside the clearance, and no outside force pushes it along the axis.
  • Left out: forces, friction values, stiffness and elastic wind-up, preload, stick-slip and wear. Drives designed to remove the clearance, such as preloaded ball nuts or adjustable split nuts, are beyond this model.
  • Illustrative: the leads, clearances and the 3D screw (5 mm lead, 1.0 mm clearance, 30° flanks) are chosen to be seen, not taken from a standard thread or a measured machine.

For drive design in depth, Alexander Slocum's Precision Machine Design (1992) covers actuators and transmissions in Chapter 10, including section 10.8, Linear Power Transmission Elements.

  1. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

    Addendum 1. Why the efficiency and strength comparisons need conditions

    The IIT Kharagpur lesson Power Screw Drives and Their Efficiency (sections 6.1.1–6.1.2, hosted by IDC) explains square-thread machining cost, trapezoidal sturdiness, and added friction from inclined flanks. Its force model supports a conditional comparison: hold lead angle, contact friction and other losses comparable. It does not establish a universal ranking against V-thread fasteners.

    Pratt & Whitney's ACME explanation describes the manufacturing and split-nut advantages. IIT Kharagpur's thread manufacturing lesson explains fastener rolling and other production routes. For thread cutting on a machine tool, see Lathe Operations.

    The buttress working flank makes efficient thrust transmission possible in its intended direction; that is a geometry-based explanation, not a promise of the same measured efficiency as square. Reverse travel is possible, but heavy loading on the opposite flank does not retain the same advantages. Compare actual screw-and-nut ratings, not shape alone.

    Back to reference 1

  2. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

    Addendum 2. Where wear and operating limits enter the selection

    Thomson: Lead Screws Q&A — Application Considerations describes sliding-contact heat and wear and the relationship between load and speed. Its discussion also distinguishes the generic lead screw from the ACME form. The absence of radial wedging does not remove contact pressure on the working flank.

  3. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

    Addendum 3. The exact standard entries used here

    NBS Circular 479, Unified Screw Thread Standards, tables 4 and 6, prints the designation entries 1/4, 20, UNC-1A and 1/4, 28, UNF-1A. The examples above omit the class suffix to teach size and pitch. This historical public standard verifies those combinations; it is not a source of current production acceptance limits. The current Unified inch thread standard is ASME B1.1-2024.

    NAAMS Metric Fastener Standards, archived sheet F–2.1, dated 05/29/15, lists M6 x1.0 under screw size and M6 x 1.0 under nominal thread diameter and pitch. Only that designation is used here. ISO 261 identifies the general-purpose metric M-thread family; its catalog entry is not being used as a dimension table.

    Back to reference 3

  4. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

    Addendum 4. Direction reference

    IIT Kharagpur: Friction in Screws, opening page, defines right-handed advance using clockwise rotation away from the person turning the screw. This observer convention avoids ambiguous arrows.

    Back to reference 4

  5. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Lead Screws

    Addendum 5. Check the definition, not just the label on a catalog

    Thomson: Screw Pitch and Lead defines lead as nut travel per screw revolution and states the pitch-times-starts relationship. A supplier may list lead directly. Do not multiply a value already labelled lead by the number of starts a second time.

    Back to reference 5

  6. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Lead Screws

    Addendum 6. Derive the 2π from equal power, or one revolution of work

    Ideally, power in equals power out: Tω = Fv. With n in rpm, ω = 2πn/60 rad/s and v = nL/60. Cancel n/60 at nonzero steady speed to get F = 2πT/L. Equivalently, one revolution puts in work 2πT and moves the load through L, doing work FL.

    With losses, Fv = ηTω. The motion ratio stays fixed, so the reduction appears in force. See Power and Efficiency. At zero speed both powers are zero; this derivation does not predict breakaway torque or static holding capacity. Lowering a load that drives the screw requires a different friction analysis.

    IIT Kharagpur: Power Screw Drives and Their Efficiency, section 6.1.2, relates output work, input work and friction. The calculator uses a given efficiency, not a friction coefficient or a thread-strength model.

    Back to reference 6

  7. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Backlash and Lost Motion

    Addendum 7. Where the definition comes from

    Modern Machine Shop's column Eliminate Backlash From Machining Centers (Mike Lynch, 2000) defines backlash as “any non-movement that occurs during axis reversals.” This page uses the CourseWiki definition on Screw Threads: clearance that must be taken up after reversing before the load moves. In a real drive, elastic deflection can add lost motion as well; the lab below leaves it out.

    Back to reference 7

  8. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Backlash and Lost Motion

    Addendum 8. A readout that measures the slide, and when the clearance still matters

    The MIT 2.670 milling machine notes (section “Using the Micrometer Dials”) also point out that a digital readout measures the bed position directly, so its reading is not thrown off by backlash. The clearance is still in the drive. A force that pushes the carriage along the screw can move it across the clearance without the handwheel turning; Climb and Conventional Milling explains when a cutting force does that.

    Back to reference 8
